newsitem.title: BOSNIA: Bosnians welcome continued NATO presence.
newsitem.headline: Bosnians welcome continued NATO presence.

text.p: Sarajevans on Thursday welcomed news that NATO troops are likely to extend their peacekeeping mission to Bosnia after the current mandate expires in December.

A decision on Wednesday by the North Atlantic alliance to instruct its military authorities to start work on a possible new peacekeeping force was hailed as an essential means of preventing a new war in Bosnia.
"NATO forces should stay in Bosnia for the next five or six years," said Djuzida Sijercic, a 60-year-old housewife.
"There is no peace and security without their presence," she told Reuters. "They have brought us peace and they should stay here to watch over that peace."

Emir Kulovic, a 73-year-old pensioner who lived through the capital's 43-month siege by Bosnian Serb forces, said feelings of animosity between the former warring factions were still too strong to allow the peacekeepers to leave.
"A strong international force is necessary to prevent a fresh outbreak of fighting in Bosnia. If they leave, a new war will erupt," he said.

Ever since it was announced that IFOR would stay for just a year, Bosnians have been sceptical that a peacekeeping mission could complete its work in such a short time after such a long and bitter war.
A Sarajevo joke asks what force will succeed IFOR? The answer: "IFIVE".
Prime Minister Hasan Muratovic also predicts a continued NATO presence, saying the future of postwar Bosnia will only become clearer after the next round of elections in two years' time.
"There is a necessity for foreign troops here for a period which cannot be foreseen now," he said.

Despite almost a year of peace in Bosnia, tension remains high, with the Serb, Moslem and Croat former combatants intensely suspicious of each other. And despite general elections last September, political institutions have been unable to start their work properly due to ethnic rivalries.
The exact shape of a peacekeeping force to follow on from the current 58,000-strong NATO-led peace Implementation Force, known as IFOR, is not yet clear.

There have been suggestions that the new force will be about half the size of IFOR, with German army combat units playing a major role in Bosnia for the first time since the Nazi occupation of World War Two.
A Reuter straw poll on the streets of Sarajevo on Thursday morning failed to find a single person who wanted IFOR to leave when its mandate expires in December.
Shopworker Arifa Kubur, aged 30, said: "Who knows what might happen. Let them stay. I just want them around and then I feel safe."
Student Mersiha Sehanovic, 22, added: "They are the only guarantee for a lasting peace. A new outbreak of fighting is inevitable without their presence."
Semir, a 24-year-old fellow student, agreed: "I'm sure we would have a new war here if they leave."
